course_description:
This course provides an introduction to the physics of lasers, atom-light interactions, and the quantization of the electromagnetic field. The implications for the conceptual foundations of quantum mechanics and nonclassical effects which arise will be considered.

Atomic physics and quantum optics have been at the heart of many of the most profound theoretical and experimental advances in quantum physics over the past 50 years. The development of lasers, laser spectroscopy, precision measurement, and coherent control of atoms has transformed our understanding of light–matter interactions and enabled major advances in quantum information science, quantum technologies, tests of fundamental physics, and searches for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

This course is organised into four main themes:

(i) Foundations of quantum optics.

Semiclassical and quantum descriptions of light; quantisation of the electromagnetic field; quantum states of light; quantum theory of coherence; interaction of atoms with quantised light, including the Jaynes–Cummings model; photon statistics, antibunching, and other non-classical states of light; and methods for describing open quantum systems.

(ii) Applications of quantum optics.

Experimental techniques in quantum optics, including laser cooling and trapping, atom–light interactions, quantum measurement, quantum communication, quantum information processing, and quantum computing, together with fundamental tests of quantum mechanics.

(iii) Foundations of atomic physics.

Atomic structure and spectra, including hydrogen-like and many-electron atoms; fine structure, hyperfine structure, and isotope shifts; angular momentum theory; spherical tensor operators; electromagnetic transition amplitudes; selection rules; and modern theoretical methods for describing atomic structure and interactions.

(iv) Applications of atomic physics.

Applications of atomic physics to precision spectroscopy, atomic clocks and frequency standards, tests of fundamental symmetries, parity violation, searches for permanent electric dipole moments, and precision searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.

course_aims: This course aims to give students an understanding of how light and matter interact, from both semiclassical and quantum points of view. Students will be introduced to the theory of atomic and molecular physics as well as quantum optics, and gain an understanding of their application to some important current research endeavours, such as high precision metrology, quantum information, and tests of fundamental physics.

learning_outcomes.description: Understand the quantum formalism used to describe the properties of atoms and molecules.
Calculate features of atomic and molecular systems such as emission spectra, energy level structure and allowed transitions.
Describe and apply both semiclassical and quantum theories of atom-light interaction, recognising their respective domains of applicability.
Recognise and quantitatively describe the kinds of optical phenomena that classical theories of light cannot predict.
Understand how the electromagnetic field can be quantized, and be able to describe mathematically some important quantum states of light.
Use the formalism of quantum optics to solve problems relating to the manipulation of the quantum states of light.
Describe the typical kinds of optical elements used in quantum optics experiments and their role in manipulating the state of light.

Understand the application of atomic and molecular physics as well as quantum optics to some important current research endeavours, such as high precision metrology, quantum information, and tests of fundamental physics.
